title: Extended Integer Types and Fixed-Width Integer Families
learningObjectives: Distinguish the standard signed and unsigned integer types from optional exact-width typedefs.
Explain the purpose of int8_t, uint16_t, uint32_t and uint64_t when provided.
Use least-width, fast-width and maximum-width integer typedef families appropriately.
Select matching format macros from inttypes.h for fixed-width values.
Check availability and range requirements instead of assuming every typedef exists.

understand.concept: The header stdint.h defines optional exact-width integer typedefs when the implementation can provide types with the requested width and no padding bits. It also provides least-width, fast-width and maximum-width integer families. Exact-width types are useful for binary formats and external interfaces, but they are not guaranteed to exist on every conforming implementation. The inttypes.h header provides portable format macros for printing many of these types.
understand.whyItMatters: Understanding Extended integer types and fixed-width integer families helps you reason about program behaviour instead of memorizing syntax. It is useful in exams, debugging and building reliable C applications.
understand.analogy: Treat the concept as a tool with a precise contract: it has valid inputs, defined operations and observable results.
understand.analogyLimit: An analogy is only an aid; the C standard and the relevant function specifications determine actual behaviour.

explain.narrative:
## 1. Why fixed-width types exist

Ordinary types such as int and long have implementation-dependent sizes and ranges. When a protocol, file format or hardware register requires an exact number of value bits, a type such as uint32_t may express that requirement more clearly—if the implementation provides it.

## 2. Exact-width typedefs

The optional typedefs include int8_t, uint8_t, int16_t, uint16_t, int32_t, uint32_t, int64_t and uint64_t. The exact-width typedefs are provided only when the implementation supports the exact width without padding bits. Do not assume that every name is always available.

## 3. Least-width and fast-width families

Types such as int_least32_t and uint_least32_t provide at least the requested width. Types such as int_fast16_t and uint_fast16_t provide a type intended to be efficient for at least that width. intmax_t and uintmax_t represent the widest supported signed and unsigned integer types.

## 4. Print values portably

Use the macros from inttypes.h rather than guessing a printf format. For example, PRIu32 is the conversion fragment for a uint32_t value when uint32_t is provided. Include the required headers and follow the macro concatenation pattern in the example.

## 5. Choose based on the contract

Use ordinary integer types for ordinary calculations when their range is sufficient. Use exact-width types when an external representation requires an exact width, and check that the implementation supplies the type. Use least-width or fast-width families when the requirement is a minimum width rather than an exact binary layout.

examples.title: Print an exact-width unsigned integer
examples.explanation: If the implementation provides uint32_t, PRIu32 supplies the matching printf conversion. Exact-width typedefs are optional when the implementation cannot provide the required representation.

examples.title: Use a minimum-width integer type
examples.explanation: The least-width family guarantees at least the requested width. The fast-width family selects an implementation's preferred efficient type with at least that width. These types are not necessarily exactly 32 or 16 bits.
